utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. McCloskey, the Chamber was informed that there was a brief preliminary matter to be raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, good morning. Good morning, everyone. I just wanted to notify you I've spoken to the Defence and we have agreed to notify you of your question regarding P2126. This was a 15 July intercept where the term "parcels" was in quote, 3500 parcels, and your question was how did that occur. Well, we found that on page 5478 of the Popovic transcript. We had put on the intercept operator that had taken that intercept and he was asked by the Prosecution how those quotes ended up in the final version, and unfortunately he said he didn't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Meanwhile, I'll deal with the following: On the 18th of July, the Chamber issued its decision on the Prosecution's 9th motion to admit evidence pursuant to Rule 92 bis as a public decision. The Chamber was subsequently notified by the Prosecution that a witness discussed in the decision might request protective measures and on the 19th of July the Chamber ordered the Registry to provisionally place the decision under seal pending the outcome of such an application. On the 30th of August, 2013, the Chamber granted the requested protective measures, which included the use of a pseudonym and the Chamber therefore instructs the Registry to make the decision permanently confidential.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler. You are reminded again that you're bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the next 3600 seconds, you'll be further examined by Mr. McCloskey. Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us a brief synopsis of your analysis regarding the events from 17 July through about 19 but specifically regarding your conclusions related to the concern the VRS had for the so-called local workers for MSF? Can you tell us briefly what you saw happen or what you take happened from the -- some of the materials and then we'll go through a couple of those materials to highlight what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. There are a number of documents and intercepts which relate to the circumstances by which the VRS, VRS government and MSF were interacting, as the MSF organisation was attempting to leave the now empty enclave. The primary concern at least as far as the VRS was concerned, was that there were a number of individuals who were described as local staff members of MSF who fell in the category that the VRS noted as able bodied Muslim men, and there was a number of discussions as to whether or not those individuals should be allowed to accompany the international staff as well as other local staff members who were female or who were elderly out with the main body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the decision process to -- what to do with these able bodied men, was there any indications that General Tolimir and General Mladic were involved in that decision?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Some of the intercepts reflect the fact that an awareness by senior members of the VRS specifically Colonel Jankovic, other members of the Main Staff, General Tolimir, that there was a current process in place that they were interested in seeing accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in the end, those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, you started by answering, "Yes, sir," where the question focused on General Tolimir and General Mladic. Now, in your answer you referred to General Tolimir but not anymore to General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. One of the documents that you'll note as an intercept refers to the procedure and again the euphemism, "the boss," being discussed by various Main Staff members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. In the end, those able bodied men were allowed to leave and did survive?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to P1374, and confidential, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we'll see -- we see that this is an intercept, and from your knowledge, do you know this to be 17 July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see that it's between Trivic and Colonel Jankovic and Badem is mentioned. And we see if we go down in the middle of it, we see that Trivic tells Jankovic that, You should write what you want to do. Jankovic says, Yes, and send it urgently by code up to Tolimir. Jankovic says, I'm in no position to write. I'm culling here and there is listen to what I'm telling you, Jankovic says, All right. Trivic says, And the commander will decide with Tolimir and send you a reply. Now, this obviously doesn't tell us what they are interested in, but who do you take the commander to be in this context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would take the commander to be General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And based on the other documents you've looked at, what do you believe this is a reference to, what is Jankovic concerned about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Jankovic at this time was dealing with issues related to, first, as you're aware he was relating to issues with the wounded Muslim men who were still in Bratunac under -- at the Bratunac medical centre under UN supervision, and then of course later he's -- in this particular context he's also dealing with the situation with the personnel from MSF.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's now go to P01515, if we could go to page 2 in e-court and should be page 3 initially in the B/C/S and then page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a document the Trial Chamber has seen before where the typed version was in the name of Momir Nikolic and we've now gone to the handwritten version which we see is RJ, and who do you take that RJ to mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those initials correspond to Colonel Jankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And if we could go to the next page in the B/C/S, and under paragraph 3, we can see some of what you've been talking about, and paragraph 3 starts off with MSF, and a convoy and then it says, Will you please tell me what stand to take in terms of authorisation for evacuation of the international organisation, MSF, in fact, how to deal with the so-called local staff. And it says this also applies to the interpreters of the military monitors and UNPROFOR. Is that the issue we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to an intercept, P00031, that the Trial Chamber has also seen through an MSF nurse a long time ago, and we see that this is dated 19 July, and at 1432 hours, and it's between Jankovic and Colonel Djurdjic. Can you remind us who Colonel Djurdjic is, what his job was?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, Colonel Djurdjic is an officer of the Main Staff whose portfolio covers dealing with the various international organisations, at least within the context that the VRS dealt with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we can see in this Jankovic and Djurdjic start speaking to each other and Djurdjic says, Regarding what you were asking, and then says, The boss has ordered that they be halted. Who do you think the boss would be in that context?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again both of these officers are members of the Main Staff so I would take it that the boss at this particular case would be their superior which would be General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what do you -- as you go on in this intercept, what do you believe Djurdjic is referring to, what should be halted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What should be halted was allowing the military age Muslim men to depart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And let's just take a look at this. It says, Djurdjic goes on to say, This is what he wrote. And who would the "he" be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again the same superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then he mentions Kristina Smit and various -- another person. Go on to the next page in English. And sorry, it should be page 3 in the B/C/S, and as we see this it goes in and says, What about those young men. And what do you take those to mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I take that to be the military-age Bosnian Muslim men who were part of the MSF local staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then they start talking about a list of various Muslim men. And then down the page, Djurdjic says, All right, they have the permission but you have the procedure, you too took part in. Then Jankovic says, Great, they don't hear each other very well. Then Djurdjic says, The procedure is such, God damn it, that it should be checked whether these who are the able bodied or older than 60. Jankovic says, They are able bodied. Djurdjic says, They are? Jankovic says, Yes. Djurdjevic says, So that's the procedure. Please go to the next page. And Djurdjevic says, And you saw what you left behind in Bratunac the other day. What do you believe that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Jankovic was present in Bratunac during the -- from at least the period of the 12th through this particular day, so he would have firsthand knowledge of the separation of the military age men that occurred in Potocari and what happened to them in Bratunac and what happened to them subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then they we can see after that they talk about an orphan, a small kid, some elderly people, then down near the end, the last part of the page, Djurdjic says, Let the elderly go and tonight when Tosa arrives you and him must sure you consult some more, please. What do you take that to involve or mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this particular context I'm not sure and I don't believe that General Tolimir actually went to Bratunac. I take it to believe that General Tolimir in this context was coming back to the Main Staff headquarters and this instruction was that when General Tolimir arrived back to the Main Staff headquarters, Colonel Jankovic should again call him and discuss the issue further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's all I wanted to do with this particular topic. Now, another topic I'd like to go to, briefly, is that I know you have spoken at length about the security branch, how the security branch functioned in relation to military-legal matters dealing with military police, dealing with prisoners of war. You've already talked a bit about that. And if we could go to 65 ter 5809. Have you identified documents -- certain documents that helped show how the security organ dealt with the issues of counter-intelligence, military legal, to help their basic -- help define the basic job in this -- and this is a document from 29 January 1995, from General Zivanovic talking about the changes in the organisation of the VRS security and intel support. If we could go to the second page, we can see in paragraph 2 there is a very brief description of how command works and how the -- some of the other basics. Also down at the bottom of the English paragraph 5 it refers to a 28 October Main Staff instruction. Does this document help identify -- help explain a bit that instruction which the Court has seen before in depth, and I won't go over that with you, that is P1577, that instruction that's referenced there. Just briefly, Mr. Butler, does this help in understanding the process, the security organ processes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Especially with relation to how they apply in the Drina Corps. As I've indicated in my prior testimony in this issue, the VRS did by and large adopt the regulations and the practices of the former Yugoslav National Army and that included an extensive body of rules and regulations pertaining to the security branches of the various armed forces and the JNA. Throughout the course of the war, in order to make these bodies more efficiently run and to deal with issue that were cropping up during the war, the Main Staff published guidance in the form of orders and other technical documents reminding the corps and the brigades about what the specific roles and functions are of the security organs, and that they should try and use these organs precisely as defined in the regulations to the degree that they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05809 receives number P2133, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we now go to 65 ter 5810.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, this, you'll see, is a document from the Drina Corps chief of security, Vujadin Popovic, dated 7 February 1995. And he's speaking on the specifics related to the military police. We see paragraph 1 is number 1, is called the command of the military police; 2, level of training; 3, mobilisation. I don't think we need to go through the entire document but does this document from Popovic help understand how a corps security branch officer deals with and is associated with military police?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does. When we talk about the issues of -- you know, one of the issues we talk about the various years and proceedings related to Srebrenica of the role and functions and authorities of various security branch officers in relation to the authorities and responsibilities of commanders, one of the things that we note that is occurring in accordance with the regulations is that the security officers are giving orders that are limited to what they are allowed to under the regulations to provide technical guidance and technical direction. This particular document is essentially a request by the corps security officer to the various brigades to examine how they have historically been using their military police forces, provide examples, and then the corps will send that information back to the Main Staff which is doing a larger analysis as to the global use of military police units by the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I offer that documents into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05810 receives number P2134, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we go to 65 ter 4183.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly speak closer to the microphone, please? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And Mr. Butler, this is a 15 April 1995 document from the Drina Corps command security department in the name of the chief of security, Vujadin Popovic, and it regards the arrest and detention of POWs and is an instruction. We see that it's directed to various brigades of the Drina Corps including the 5th Military Police Battalion. And we see this has to do with prisoners of war and I don't want to get into this in detail but does this document on its face help us show us how a -- the corps security chief deal with issues related to POWs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I mean, here again, he's providing guidance as to the handling procedures of POWs in order to ensure that information that might be of security interest to the opposing forces can be protected and not disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do we note in paragraph 1, which should be the next page in the English, that prisoners of war should be -- have their hands tied and be blindfolded basically as we look on to prevent their escape and to prevent their ability to look at military secrets on the front lines as they are taken back to the rear. Does this help us understand the relationship between the prisoners and the security officer?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04183 receives number P2135, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, now I'd also like if you could discuss briefly a section that you've spoken about before, that we refer generally as the Milici patients, where some 10 to 15 or thereabouts Muslim men were captured in the Nova Kasaba area and were treated and were placed in the Milici hospital. Can you basically tell us what the documents have -- again very briefly then we will go through some of the documents, to show what you based your analysis on?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. One of the issues that -- and as I talked about I believe last week that I looked at was case histories of individuals who were known to be in the custody of the Army of the Republika Srpska and subsequently are now listed on the ICRC missing list or were back in the day. This group of prisoners who were injured was documented as being treated in Milici and at some point of time was transferred from Milici to the hospital in Zvornik. They were subsequently transferred from the hospital in Zvornik to the medical centre at the Standard barracks of the Zvornik Brigade, and from the barracks of the Zvornik Brigade they subsequently disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to 65 ter 5128. And this is a 24 July 1995 document, and you see it's Republika Srpska Svetinakova [phoen] war hospital in Milici, Drina Corps command, to General Radislav Krstic personally. And if we can -- it's from the war hospital director Dr. Radomir Davidovic, neurosurgeon. And he talks about various issues associated with the events of early July and later. And if we he could go to page 2, and looking at -- near the bottom of the page, it says, 18 wounded enemy have undergone surgery and have been transferred to the hospital in Zvornik on the orders of the Main Staff. How does this fit into what you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It dove tails with our ability to track these individuals as they were initially treated in Milici and of course we have copies of the hospital records reflecting that, and the fact that on the orders of the Main Staff, they were transferred from the Milici hospital to the Zvornik hospital for follow-on treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05128 receives number P2136, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now could we go to 65 ter 5130.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, this is a short listing of Muslim names, and is it your understanding that these are some of the men that were -- did undergo surgery and were treated at the Milici hospital and then were sent on to the Zvornik hospital?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is a copy or a translation of the copy of the intake log of the Milici medical centre identifying the individual patients and year of birth and their residence, as well as the reason for their admittance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I would offer that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05130 receives number P2137, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we go to 65 ter 5132. This should also be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, as we'll soon be able to see that this is a stack of patient records indicating the condition of the various patients and how serious some of them were injured. Are these the patients in question, to your understanding, and their records from Milici?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer these records into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05132 receives number P2138, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence, under seal as well. Yes, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to P2130.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a document we have just seen but I want to ask you something specifically about it. It is an interim combat report from Vinko Pandurevic on 22 July. And we see here that to remind us, this is where Vinko Pandurevic is asking the command for instructions on what to do with prisoners, where to put them and whom they should hand them over to, and we'll recall your answer on that. Let's go to an intercept on -- for the next day, 23 July. It's 65 ter 21164C, of 23 July. Mr. Butler, as you look at this intercept between Pandurevic and an unknown person, do you recall that this is a 23 July intercept?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we can see that Pandurevic states here that, We are catching Turks still, I have prisoners, I have the wounded, so I don't know what to do with them, where to send them. This reference to wounded, at this time do you know, does he have the Milici wounded?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. At this time they are in the medical clinic of the Zvornik Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And while we won't go through them, have you seen information regarding the transfer of those people from Zvornik down to the Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then Vinko says, Yes, yes, so who should I transport these to, does anyone know? And Vinko says, So what about Matkovic? Do you have an opinion what Matkovic may be?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that individual as a name. It could be referring to Batkovic which is the larger detention centre but it's unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then he says, Because the memo has arrived that the wounded be sent to the hospital in Zvornik but there is a problem with this so I would ask that some solution be found for it today. And what do you believe that's a reference to?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware, as of course -- of the investigation, that there was a great reluctance by the people of Zvornik to have these Muslims in the hospital there. They were initially sent to the hospital in Zvornik from Milici and the reason why they were then sent to Standard barracks was because the local population felt very uncomfortable about having them there. So an order to send them back to the hospital in Zvornik would again re-raise that same issue of the population not wanting them there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Same standard objection to the intercepts, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 21164C receives number P2139, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's under that number that the intercept is admitted into evidence - please proceed - under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could now go to another intercept, should be under seal, 65 ter number 21162A.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This from your investigation would also have been identified as 23 July, and this one is now at 805, five minutes after the last one. And we'll see here that it's one of those brief little summaries that says the participant in the previous conversation called and asked for Vinko again but Ljubo answered and question mark told Ljubo to pass on to Vinko, What Vinko and I were just talking about will arrive at your place by 1700 hours, the boss, Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, will arrive and say what needs to be done regarding the work we talked about. How does this fit into these wounded?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this intercept is related to that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in this particular context, I mean the issue that they were referring to, the being the wounded Muslims and the fact Colonel Popovic is a security officer. In the context of what happens to these individuals afterwards, it is fairly clear why Popovic is going up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why do you think?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the individuals are missing. Colonel Popovic was historically associated with issues relating to the execution and burial of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What reason, if any, would the VRS have into executing several seriously injured people that were taken from the area of Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Matter of speculation. I don't know whether the VRS was concerned that they saw something or knew something. I mean, there are -- there are no technically lawful rationales that can be provided so, I mean, you could speculate for quite a long time as to why they thought these people would need to be liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's not speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to P1501. I'm sorry, thank you. I would like that into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Same objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 21162A receives number P2140, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence - the objection is overruled - under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And perhaps to save a bit of time I'll just refer you, Mr. Butler, and the Trial Chamber, that I was -- that last references to the duty officer notebook for 23 July with a notation at 0830 hours, Lieutenant-Colonel Cerovic relayed a message for the commander that Lieutenant Colonel Popovic will arrive by 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that notation in the duty officer notebook related to the intercept you just saw?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I believe it confirms that intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And there is a document that's already into evidence, D341, it is the vehicle log for Vujadin Popovic that shows a trip on his vehicle on the 23rd of July from Vlasenica to Zvornik to Vlasenica. Is that consistent with Popovic going to Zvornik, as this is noted here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you do so, Mr. McCloskey, could I invite you to reorganise P2137, which is the hospital log. It starts with an undated page having entries 11, 12, 13, 14, and then the second page is 1 to 10. I think the logical order would be e-court pages 2 plus 3 first and then after that, 1 and 4. Could you reorganise it so that it makes sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, please. I hopefully speculate that that's the order we picked it up from the hospital in but I may be wrong on that. The hospital -- it may be us. So we'll fix that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. Butler, you've already spoken briefly on some documents that show General Tolimir was concerning himself with the large number of prisoners first at Nova Kasaba on the 13th, and then suggesting some could be moved to Rogatica. Have you seen documents in your study that indicate General Tolimir was involved with the exchange of large numbers of prisoners from early on in the war?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. General Tolimir specifically, and the VRS security organs in general, were interested in the issue, not only of prisoners and their security but also the fact that prisoners that they had captured could be used in order to trade against the other side to return Bosnian Serb soldiers who had been captured or were detained by the Muslim or Croatian side so there was always this keen interest during the course of the conflict to capture enemy soldiers so they could get enough soldiers that they could effectively trade back and get their own captured people back, returned to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's quickly go through some of these, 65 ter 23647, and I think they are largely self-explanatory so I would just like for you to either confirm or deny that these fit your analysis on General Tolimir's interest in prisoners and exchange. So, first, 65 ter 23647. We see this is a 25 October 1993 document, the second page is Zdravko Tolimir and we see the initials LJB. Who do you think the initials were? And I believe we've heard evidence that those would be the initials of the person that drafted the report.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, those initials, to my knowledge, correspond to Colonel Ljubisa Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And does this document have to do with the exchange of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would -- no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 23647 receives number P2141, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2141 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we now have 65 ter 23811.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we'll see, as this comes up, Mr. Butler, this is another document from the Main Staff in the name of Zdravko Tolimir, this time drafted by ZT, Zdravko Tolimir, to the intelligence department of the Drina Corps entitled: "Exchange of prisoners." Does this also -- is this also a document that you looked at in determining the interest and job of General Tolimir to be involved with prisoners and prisoner exchanges?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 23811 receives number P2142, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2142 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And 65 ter 23863.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We'll see again a document from General Tolimir dated 20 January 1995 now to the intelligence and security section of the Drina Corps, and East Bosnia Corps, entitled: "Prisoner exchange." Is this another such document that you looked at to determine General Tolimir's job in prisoner exchanges?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 23863 receives number P2143, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 4173.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is the last such document, Mr. Butler. And this is another document from General Tolimir now, 29 July, after some of our Srebrenica events and is referring to the disarmament of the 1st Zepa Brigade. If we could go to page 2 in the English, still B/C/S page 1, and could you blow up that B/C/S so it could be read, on the third big -- third paragraph down we see that there is a reference to continued combat operation in order to surround and destroy the 1st Zepa Brigade until the Muslims make the exchange and carry out the agreement from 24 July related to their disarmament and surrender, take all necessary measures to prevent them from leaving the encirclement. This is the sentence I want to ask you about, it says: Do not register persons you capture before cessation of fire and do not report them to international organisations. We are going to keep them for exchange in case the Muslims do not carry out the agreement or they manage to break through from the encirclement. This order not to register people or make lists of them, is that appropriate military conduct in your view?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I would offer this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 04173 receives number P2144, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, you have spoken of the restriction of convoys both to UNPROFOR and to the enclave population itself and I would like to go over just a couple of the examples of the material that you may have looked at in going -- coming to those conclusions. Could we go to 65 ter 24841. And, Mr. Butler, without going through the details of this document we can see that -- what this is. Can you tell us briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. This is the response of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska to UNPROFOR Sarajevo letting them know which convoys from their larger request that they did not authorise for passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we see for Srebrenica number 7 and number 12, and did you incorporate the review of this document for your analysis regarding the convoy restrictions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. While it was not part of my report per se, with these documents, I have testified about these extensively in previous trials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This material came in after your time here?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd offer that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24841 receives number P2145, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2145 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could we now go to 65 ter 24848.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We see this is the heading of the Main Staff, it's to the UNPROFOR Command Sarajevo. Number 1, we have not approved the movement of a convoy number from Srebrenica into Banja Koviljaca because the discrepancy between the number of people entering and exiting Srebrenica. Is this something, another document you reviewed in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would offer that document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 24848 receives number P2146, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2146 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And 65 ter 5535, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Butler, we see this is a bit different. It's still from the Main Staff in the name of Lieutenant-General Milovanovic, and this is to the commands of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and Drina Corps, and let me read that first sentence which is a bit blotted out by the draft translation. It's, Please be informed we have not approved movement of the following UNPROFOR convoys and teams. Can you confirm, Mr. Butler, that that's what it says underneath there, from your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is this another, let's -- we can see number 4, well, actually let's go to the next page in the English, numbered page 2 in the English. We see under number 9, a reference to Srebrenica, 8 April, comprising seven vehicles and 18 persons which were supposed to transport diesel fuel. We told them they had 79 tonnes of fuel with Oric. So they were refusing this request. What do you make, if anything, of this reference about Oric?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sir, one of the allegations that the VRS did level against the UNPROFOR was that they were not only carrying humanitarian goods or things of that nature, but that the ABiH was using the UNPROFOR as a way to smuggle in material, weapons and fuel, in for the ABiH military purposes. Again, in this particular context, their concern that fuel that is supposed to be going to UNPROFOR somehow gets diverted to Naser Oric and is used for military purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, we have mostly seen references to UNPROFOR convoys. Were there also convoys that the humanitarian -- for the humanitarian organisations, UNHCR and the ICRC and others?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did the VRS have any control over those convoys?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And could I tender that last document into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 05535 receives number P2147, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, did you and I go over this binder of basic convoy materials prior to your testifying?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The particular binder that you're holding is a grouping of a number of documents which relate to various requests by UNPROFOR and various international organisations to request to move goods to people throughout Eastern Bosnia as well as the replies from the VRS and other organs that had control over whether they could access or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did each of those documents fit into your conclusion regarding the convoy restrictions overseen and controlled by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD BUTLER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am done. I would like to offer the 13 remaining documents in bulk as referred to by Mr. Butler. I can get a list. I've mentioned this to the Defence before. I'm not sure of their feelings on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was mentioned yesterday afternoon. I believe that if documents are going to be tendered through a witness, the witness has to provide testimony as to the documents and has to identify the documents. Referring to a "binder" I don't think is an appropriate means of the witness identifying which particular documents he has referred to, so I would object to that type of a mass addition of documents by pointing to a "binder" quote unquote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Mr. Ivetic, you know that sometimes documents which are related to the testimony of a witness, although are not specifically dealt with and perhaps not specified by -- with the witness, that they are admitted from the bar table where usually we would wait until later, but if there is a direct relation to the testimony of the witness. Would you oppose a -- the tendering of those documents from the bar table in the context of the testimony of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any reason for that, in view of the practice I set out a second ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the jurisprudence in relation to bar table submissions requires that the documents be identified, their provenance be identified, and submissions be made in a bar table motion, the Defence be given adequate time to respond. That has not been followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I believe the procedure I've just laid out is, while the bar table I think a fine procedure that I'm sure both sides will use, this actually is a better procedure. Mr. Butler has referred to the 13 documents as having reviewed them and how they fit into it. You can see that these documents are very self-explanatory and simple. It would be, in my view, a waste of the Court's time to go through each one individually and have Mr. Butler tell us what time our watch says. It's right there. So it is important for the overall context to see this as a whole and for the Chamber to review when you're making this important decision. Well, I think this is an excellent way for this material to come before the Trial Chamber without the problems of filings and arguing over something in written form. It also gives the Defence a chance to cross-examine specific documents that are specifically laid out as opposed to responding in paper in a bar table. So I think this is a better way to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, the Chamber would allow for the following procedure: You make a full list of the documents you had in your mind instead of referring to a binder where of course the Chamber has got no idea of what is found in that binder, so you make a list, you give that to -- it will be provided to the witness, not directly but through Chamber, and after the witness has had a look at that list, we'll ask him whether or not he has considered those documents in -- whether he reviewed those documents in being at the basis of his testimony and his reporting. That is the way in which the Chamber suggests you proceed rather than to refer a binder with unknown content, as far as the Chamber is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This is the witness's list, and Ms. Stewart has identified in yellow the documents and the Defence has -- I sent them a separate list of only convoy documents and we've now just used three that are already now in evidence because I went over them. So I merely mention the binder so Mr. Butler would know that he's talking about something specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is -- you have not prepared specifically you've highlighted in yellow on a list. Could that first be shown to Mr. Ivetic with the assistance of the usher? And Mr. Ivetic, if there is no further comment on it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There should be no further comment, Your Honour. I trust that this is comports the list that was sent to us at 330 last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, minus the three which are admitted, I do understand. Could the list be given to the witness. Witness, could we invite you to look at the yellow highlighted items on this list and then to tell us, after the break, whether you have consulted and reviewed these documents, and whether they are in line with or consistent with your findings as reported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we take a break, Mr. McCloskey, unless there is anything else to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just simply, Mr. Butler's reports which I have lists of his reports and their annexes, it's my understanding that Mr. Ivetic would not be objecting to his three command reports but would be objecting to the narrative reports and their annexes. And as far as I'm concerned we can deal with that after the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct and I would agree with that procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's already on the record that for some reports there are no objections and for others there will be and we'll decide admission or non-admission after the cross-examination of the witness. Madam Registrar, anything to be added? No? Then could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes from now, Mr. Butler.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And needless to say, I have nothing else to say, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I did understand that this concluded your -- and I must say even with the procedural matters attached, you stayed within your 3600 seconds. We take a break and we resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not receive ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Already for several days, the past week, we have noticed that General Mladic is not able to follow, and now talking to him, we have found out that in the past few days of the last week and the week before, he has been unable to socialise with others in the Detention Unit. He's now lying down. He has no strength for anything. He can't drink or eat, and he maintains that he's so exhausted that he cannot function anymore. He explained also to the nurse today that, again, the left side of his body is numb and he has the feeling that his left arm and left leg are going to explode. And he feels enormous pressure in his hamstrings. We believe that this trial cannot continue in this way anymore. We have said before we needed one day off and now we believe it's two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I'm going to interrupt you there. We are dealing at this moment with the present situation. I do understand that Mr. Mladic has reported that he doesn't feel well. You have explained what these symptoms are he's experiencing at this moment. We also do understand that the nurse said that he should be brought back to the UNDU and the Chamber, of course, will ask for a full medical report about the findings of the doctors. The issue of the medical reports and whether that justifies to postpone or to sit four days a week are at this moment before the Appeals Chamber. Any additional motions in this respect, accompanied by supporting medical reports, will be taken very seriously by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until now, they have never been seriously considered by the Chamber. The Chamber acted counter to the instructions of the doctors. I'm telling you General Mladic, contrary to my own instructions, came to attend this trial. I shall not allow this anymore. Instead, when he's unable to follow the trial, I will not allow him to be present anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether that is within your competence but not to be discussed at this very moment. I leave it to what I just said. At this moment, I do understand that Mr. Mladic has not waived his right to be present at trial, which means that we will adjourn and wait for the medical reports and see how we -- and when we will continue. I would expect that the Chamber would receive, Madam Registrar, a first medical report this afternoon so that we are -- so that we know where we are for tomorrow. I'd like to ask the witness to return so as to inform him about the present situation. If there is anything you would like add, Mr. Lukic, please do so, but please keep in mind that the Chamber wants to follow a strict procedural order.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have nothing to add at this moment. We shall try to visit our client this afternoon, if we are able to organise it. We are unable to organise visits for the same day but I hope we shall meet with some understanding on the part of the Detention Unit today to see the situation of our client and to see whether we are going to be able to continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Butler, we will not continue at this moment. Mr. Mladic has reported to be unwell. The -- a member of the medical staff has decided that it would be better for him to return to the United Nations Detention Unit, and that's what happened. That means that we are a bit of uncertain about when we will be able to continue but any news will reach you through the Victims and Witness Section. Could I just inquire with you whether you have any commitments in the very near future, that is in the coming -- the last days of this week and perhaps the first days of next week which would be -- which would prevent you from continuing your testimony with some delay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, sir. I guess the one advantage of being employed with a law enforcement organisation is they more than other employers understand the necessities of court. I'm obviously available at the disposal of the Court, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That is appreciated. Is there any other matter at this moment to be raised? If not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, I do have the one document that you did ask me to look at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but we'll continue with that once the accused is back because we can't continue with the proceedings under the present circumstances, but perhaps you for your own memory you write down or you read it again or should it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I hold on to this document or should I return it to someone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think if you could keep it at this moment unless there is any problem. I see the parties both agree. If you keep it with you and whenever you restart look at it again and see whether what you have read during this break, whether that is still the same. We adjourn sine die. One second, please. Before we adjourn, Mr. Butler, I again have to instruct you not to speak or communicate in whatever way even when it's during a bit of a longer period of time with anyone about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn sine die.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 11.12 a.m. sine die 23 24 25
